meta.description: Genuine Bukowski. The closing line of his answer in LIFE magazine’s “The Meaning of Life” feature, December 1988 — and rarely quoted in full.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'We are here to laugh at the odds and live our lives so well that Death will tremble to take us'?
meta.ogDescription: Really Bukowski — the last sentence of his December 1988 LIFE magazine statement. Verified source, full paragraph, and what the reposts cut.

answer.label: Written by
answer.authorDates: 1920–1994 · American poet, novelist and short-story writer
answer.sourceLine: Genuine, and traceable to a specific page. It is the closing sentence of the short statement Bukowski contributed to LIFE magazine’s feature The Meaning of Life: The Big Picture in December 1988 — a paragraph that begins by rejecting “the God formula” and ends with this line. Wikiquote’s sourced list and the WIST quotation database both carry the full paragraph under that citation.

source.heading: The source

docMeta.dd: The Meaning of Life: The Big Picture
The Meaning of Life: Reflections in Words and Pictures on Why We Are Here (Little, Brown, 1991)

source.excerpt: For those who believe in God, most of the big questions are answered. But for those of us who can’t readily accept the God formula, the big answers don’t remain stone-written. We adjust to new conditions and discoveries. We are pliable. Love need not be a command or faith a dictum. I am my own God. We are here to unlearn the teachings of the church, state and our educational system. We are here to drink beer. We are here to kill war. We are here to laugh at the odds and live our lives so well that Death will tremble to take us.
trail: Wikiquote ↗ carries the full paragraph in its sourced material, cited to “The Meaning of Life: The Big Picture”, LIFE magazine (December 1988) — not in any misattributed or disputed section.

The WIST quotation database ↗ files the same paragraph under the same LIFE citation, and The Marginalian ↗ reproduces it in its piece on the feature and the 1991 Little, Brown book that collected the responses.

A long-running Bukowski Forum thread ↗ records readers tracking the line to that issue and posting the magazine page; contributors there disagree about the page number, so we cite the issue rather than a page.

A dealer listing for the December 1988 issue ↗ independently confirms the magazine ran the feature, describing it as a portfolio in which “philosophers, pundits and plain folk ponder what it’s all about.”
source.excerptNote: The line that circulates is the final sentence of this paragraph. Renderings differ trivially on “stone-written” / “stonewritten”; the famous sentence itself is quoted consistently and without alteration.

author.name: Charles Bukowski
author.heading: Who was Charles Bukowski?
author.metaLine: 1920–1994 · American poet, novelist and short-story writer
author.bio: Born Heinrich Karl Bukowski in Andernach, Germany, in 1920 and raised in Los Angeles, Bukowski spent much of his working life as a letter carrier and filing clerk for the U.S. Post Office, quitting in 1969 to write full time. Black Sparrow Press published nearly everything that followed — Post Office (1971), Factotum (1975), Women (1978), Ham on Rye (1982) — and by the late 1980s he was famous enough that a mass-circulation American magazine would ask him what life meant. He died in San Pedro, California, in March 1994.

misattribution.heading: Right author, wrong provenance
misattribution.intro: There is nothing wrong with the name on this one. What travels badly is everything else — where it came from, what form it was written in, and the four sentences in front of it.

items.why: Goodreads carries the line with a bare author byline and no publication at all, above its own notice that community-added quotes are not verified — which is how a line with a precise, checkable citation ends up looking rootless. See the Goodreads entry ↗.

items.who: Social posts presenting it as a Bukowski poem
items.why: It is often line-broken and posted as poetry, sometimes folded in with The Laughing Heart. It is not a poem: Wikiquote ↗ carries it as one continuous prose paragraph written for a magazine feature.

The sentences that set it up — “I am my own God” and “We are here to unlearn the teachings of the church, state and our educational system” — are almost always dropped, turning an explicitly godless credo into a generic toast. The Marginalian ↗ prints the whole answer.

misattribution.truthLine: It really is Bukowski, and it really has a citation: the closing sentence of his statement in “The Meaning of Life: The Big Picture,” LIFE, December 1988 — documented in WIST ↗ and in Wikiquote’s sourced list ↗.

context.heading: Why the full paragraph matters
lead: In 1988 the editors of LIFE put one question to roughly 300 people — the Dalai Lama, Rosa Parks, Richard Nixon, farmers, barbers — and printed the answers as a portfolio called The Meaning of Life: The Big Picture. Bukowski, then living in San Pedro and long past needing to be polite about it, sent back a paragraph that opens by ruling God out and then simply lists what is left: unlearn the church, the state and the schools; drink beer; kill war; laugh at the odds. The famous sentence is the last item on that list.

Detached, the line reads like a toast — which is why it ends up on posters, tattoos and graduation cards. In place, it is the punchline of an argument: if there is nobody to appeal to and nothing written in stone, then living well is not a reward for anything, it is the whole of the available response. The reposts almost always cut the four sentences that make that argument.
context.detailsSummary: What happened to the LIFE feature afterwards
detailsBody: The responses were gathered into a book — The Meaning of Life: Reflections in Words and Pictures on Why We Are Here, credited to David Friend and the Editors of Life and published by Little, Brown in 1991 — pairing the statements with photographs from the LIFE archive. A scan of that first edition is held by the Internet Archive.
LIFE ran the feature in December 1988. Bukowski died in March 1994, which makes this one of the last general-audience statements of his own position he ever gave.

sourcesVerified.claim: Wikiquote's sourced section for Charles Bukowski contains the full paragraph ending "...Death will tremble to take us", cited to "The Meaning of Life: The Big Picture", Life Magazine (December 1988), with no misattributed/disputed section on the page.

The WIST quotation database entry gives the same full paragraph and cites it to Life Magazine, December 1988, article "The Meaning of Life: The Big Picture", attributed to Charles Bukowski (1920-1994).

The Marginalian reproduces Bukowski's full answer verbatim and identifies the 1991 compilation "The Meaning of Life: Reflections in Words and Pictures on Why We Are Here", which collected responses from 300 people originally solicited by LIFE's editors in 1988.

A Bukowski Forum thread traces the quote to LIFE Magazine, December 1988 (an issue devoted to the 'meaning of life'), with a member posting the magazine article and another transcribing the passage from the magazine; page-number claims within the thread are inconsistent with the issue's contents listing.

The Internet Archive holds a borrowable scan of "The Meaning of life: reflections in words and pictures on why we are here" by David Friend (b. 1955), published by Little, Brown (Boston), 1991, ISBN 0316294020.

A dealer listing for the December 1988 issue of LIFE lists a feature portfolio in which "philosophers, pundits and plain folk ponder what it's all about", confirming the issue carried "The Meaning of Life" feature.
Goodreads presents the quote attributed only to "Charles Bukowski" with no book, publication or date, above its notice that community-added quotes are not verified by Goodreads.

Charles Bukowski was born 16 August 1920 in Andernach, Germany and died 9 March 1994 in San Pedro, Los Angeles; he worked for the U.S. Post Office until 1969 and was published mainly by Black Sparrow Press, with works including Post Office (1971), Factotum (1975), Women (1978) and Ham on Rye (1982).
